terminal.description: A shell in your workspace: node run.mjs <file> runs the query in that file against a fresh copy of the practice's database and prints the rows.

tasks.title: Count the owners
tasks.description:
Rosamund is filling in the practice's yearly form and needs three numbers about the owners.

In `queries/1-owner-counts.sql`, return one row from `owners` with three columns, in this order:

- `owners`: how many owners there are
- `with_email`: how many of them gave an email
- `towns`: how many different towns they live in

Check compares the columns and the row on the data you can see and on hidden data.
nextSteps: Write a query that counts every owner, name the column, and run it.
Add a second count that only counts the owners who have an email.
Add a third count that counts each town once, however many owners live there.
Compare the three numbers with what you see in `seed.sql`.
hints: Each of the three columns is a `COUNT`. What goes inside the brackets decides what is counted.
`COUNT(*)` counts rows. `COUNT(column)` skips the rows where that column is `NULL`. One more word inside the brackets counts each value once.
The columns have the shapes `COUNT(*) AS owners`, `COUNT(column) AS with_email` and `COUNT(DISTINCT column) AS towns`.

videos.title: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX

tasks.title: Sum up the treatments
tasks.description:
Rosamund wants to know what the treatments brought in.

In `queries/2-takings.sql`, return one row from `treatments` with four columns, in this order:

- `total`: the prices added up
- `average`: the average price, rounded to 2 decimal places
- `cheapest`: the lowest price
- `dearest`: the highest price

Every treatment counts, the free ones too. Check compares the columns and the row on the data you can see and on hidden data.
nextSteps: Write the four columns one at a time, running the file after each.
Look at the average: how many decimal places does it have?
Round it to 2 decimal places and run it again.
hints: Each column is one aggregate over `price`. The lesson's part "Adding up" lists them.
`ROUND` takes the number and how many decimal places to keep. It goes around the average, not inside it.
The second column has the shape `ROUND(AVG(price), 2) AS average`.

tasks.title: Find the average weight of the dogs
tasks.description:
Ifan orders worming tablets by the average weight of the dogs he sees.

In `queries/3-dog-weights.sql`, return one row from `animals` with two columns, in this order:

- `dogs`: how many dogs there are, weighed or not
- `average_kg`: the average weight of the dogs that have been weighed, rounded to 2 decimal places

A dog nobody has weighed has no weight; it does not weigh 0. Check compares the columns and the row on the data you can see and on hidden data.
nextSteps: Keep only the dogs with a condition, and count them.
Add the average weight, rounded to 2 decimal places, and run it.
Work the average out by hand from `seed.sql` for the weighed dogs and compare.
hints: One dog has no weight. Ask yourself what each of your two columns does with it.
`AVG` already skips empty cells, and `COUNT(*)` counts every row. Turning `NULL` into 0 would pull the average down.
The query has the shape `SELECT COUNT(*) AS dogs, ROUND(AVG(weight_kg), 2) AS average_kg FROM animals WHERE ...;`.

tasks.title: Total the charges over £250
tasks.description:
The insurer asks how many single charges came to more than £250, and what they added up to. Rosamund thinks there were none, and the form wants a number in both boxes.

In `queries/4-big-charges.sql`, return one row from `treatments` with two columns, in this order:

- `charges`: how many treatments cost more than £250
- `total`: their prices added up, and `0` when there are none

Check compares the columns and the row on the data you can see and on hidden data, which has charges over £250 and one of exactly £250.
nextSteps: Write the condition for a price over £250 and count the rows.
Add the total of their prices, and run it. Look hard at what the total shows.
Make the total show 0 when nothing matches.
hints: Run it: with no rows to add up, one of your two columns is not a number. The lesson's part "When nothing matches" says why.
`COALESCE`, from the issue about missing values, gives back its second value when the first is `NULL`.
The second column has the shape `COALESCE(SUM(price), 0) AS total`.
